back: Aleatoric: irreducible noise in the process. Epistemic: the model's ignorance because of limited data; shrinks with more data.
$p_k=\mathrm{softmax}(z/T)$. $T>1$ flattens (less confident), $T<1$ sharpens. The arg-max, hence accuracy, never changes.
Minimise the held-out negative log-likelihood over the single scalar $T$ (1-D search such as golden section). Never on the training set.
Fit a monotone non-decreasing map from score to probability (pool adjacent violators). Flexible but needs more data; cannot fix poor ranking.
No: a strictly increasing map of scores keeps the ranking. Calibration changes confidence, not discrimination.
Fit $B$ models on resamples with replacement; the std of their predictions at $x$ estimates the epistemic spread.
Mean of member noise variances (aleatoric) plus variance of member means (epistemic).
$S_N^{-1}=\alpha I+\beta\Phi^\top\Phi$, $m_N=\beta S_N\Phi^\top t$. The mean equals ridge with $\lambda=\alpha/\beta$.
$\sigma_N^2(x)=\beta^{-1}+\phi(x)^\top S_N\phi(x)$: noise plus parameter uncertainty. Shapes: $\phi\in\mathbb R^M$, $S_N\in\mathbb R^{M\times M}$.

front: Prediction interval vs confidence interval for the mean
back: A prediction interval covers a new observation (includes noise); a confidence interval for $f(x)$ omits the noise term and is narrower.
Fit on proper train; compute scores $s_i$ on $n$ held-out points; $\hat q$ = $\lceil (n+1)(1-\alpha)\rceil$-th smallest; interval $\hat f(x)\pm\hat q$.
Under exchangeability and no ties: $1-\alpha\le P(y\in C(x))\le 1-\alpha+1/(n+1)$, for any model.

front: Core idea of the conformal proof
back: The test score's rank among $n+1$ exchangeable scores is uniform; it is below the $k$-th calibration score with probability $k/(n+1)$.
Marginal, not conditional coverage; breaks under distribution shift or drifting time series; a poor model gives valid but wide intervals.
